rows.timeline_year_basis: The Qur'an is never dated; it is the single starting block
rows.name: Qur'an
rows.detail: Not named in the Qur'an — rests on the general permission of trade (2:275) and mutual consent (4:29).
rows.detail_long: Who: The Qur'an is the first rung of every USUL ladder: it is never dated, and every later rung refers back to it. What: Murabaha has no dedicated verse. Its legitimacy hangs on 'Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba' (2:275) and the mutual-consent rule of 4:29 — the same two verses every later cost-plus structure cites. The verses, in the translation held in the Gold Ark Library: 4:29 — “O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly but only [in lawful] business by mutual consent. And do not kill yourselves [or one another]. Indeed, Allah is to you ever Merciful.” Why here: The Qur'an opens the Murabaha ladder and is never dated. Source: Qur'an 2:275; 4:29.

hadith_meta.narrator: abu Hamzah, from Imam al-Baqir (abu Ja'far)
topics_app: Selling for Capital with an Additional Certain Percentage Profit (Murabahah)

rows.detail: Murabahah chapter. Imam al-Baqir: no murabaha resale until each item's cost basis is made clear — the disclosure rule stated by name.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kafi was compiled by al-Kulayni (864-941), a Persian Shia scholar and hadith compiler. Narrator: abu Hamzah, from Imam al-Baqir (abu Ja'far). What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: a man buys goods in bulk, prices each piece to cover capital, then wants to sell 'in the form of Murabahah (capital plus a certain percent profit)'. The Imam: 'No, he cannot do so until he makes it clear that the item has a fixed price.' The cost-transparency core of murabaha, in a chapter titled for it. The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: “1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Muhammad ibn Aslam from abu Hamzah who has said the following: “I once asked abu Ja’far (a.s.), about the case of a man who buys goods altogether for a certain price, then sets a price for each piece proportionately until all of his capital is covered; if he can sell it in the form of Murabahah (capital plus a certain percent profit). He (the Imam) said, ‘No, he cannot do so until he makes it clear that the item has a fixed price.’”” It stands in Selling for Capital with an Additional Certain Percentage Profit (Murabahah) or a Certain Amount of Profit with Mention of Percentage Ratio. Why here: 'Imami reports (Shia line)' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 941 (compilation date: al-Kafi compiled by al-Kulayni (d.941, standard reference); report attributed to Imam al-Baqir (d.~732)). Source: Al-Kafi vol.5, hadith 694.

hadith_meta.narrator: Maysir the fabric seller, from Imam al-Sadiq (Abu Abdullah)

rows.detail: Murabaha on credit. Imam al-Sadiq: goods bought on credit and resold as murabaha carry the same credit period to the buyer — cost disclosure includes the terms.
rows.detail_long: Who: Man la yahduruh al-Faqih was compiled by Ibn Babawayh, known as al-Shaykh al-Saduq (923-991), a Shia scholar, jurist and hadith collector. Narrator: Maysir the fabric seller, from Imam al-Sadiq (Abu Abdullah). What: The report, as held in the Gold Ark Library: the fabric-seller buys merchandise on credit, states its valuation, sells at profit. The Imam rules: 'If you sell it on a profit basis (Murabaha), then he is entitled to the same credit period as you.' Murabaha's honesty duty covers not just price but how it was financed. The report (opening), as held in the Gold Ark Library: “Hadith.3794 - Maysir, the seller of fabrics, narrated: I said to Abu Abdullah (as): We purchase merchandise on credit, and a man comes and asks, "For how much was it valued for you?" I reply, "It was valued at such and such," and then I sell it to him at a profit. [...]” It stands in Chapter on Sales. Why here: 'Imami reports (Shia line)' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 991 (compilation date: Ibn Babawayh al-Saduq (d.991, standard reference); report attributed to Imam al-Sadiq). Source: Man la yahduruh al-Faqih vol.3, hadith 677 / 3794.

rows.name: Ibn Abbas (attrib., Tanwir al-Miqbas)
rows.detail: The earliest attributed gloss on 2:275: deferred-sale increase is permitted trade; increase on a due debt is the forbidden riba.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abd Allah ibn Abbas (618-686) was a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, remembered as the 'Scholar of the Umma' and highly regarded for his knowledge of traditions and his interpretation of the Qur'an. The commentary Tanwir al-Miqbas is attributed to him by tradition; the attribution is traditional, not critical, which is why the work is marked 'attrib.' What: Tanwir al-Miqbas on 2:275 reads the deniers' claim 'trade is just like usury' as equating increase at the START of a deferred sale with increase when the term FALLS DUE — and the verse's answer: Allah permits the former (trading) and forbids the latter (usury). The exact line every cost-plus (murabaha) structure stands on. Attribution to Ibn Abbas is traditional, not critical — hence 'attrib.' Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 687 (death of Ibn Abbas, to whom the work is attributed). Source: Tanwir al-Miqbas (attrib. Ibn Abbas), on Q2:275.

rows.name: al-Tabari
rows.detail: Al-Tabari's commentary on 2:275 fixes the trade-versus-riba distinction murabaha rests on.
rows.detail_long: Who: Abu Ja'far al-Tabari (839-923) was a Sunni scholar, historian, jurist and Qur'an commentator from Amol in Tabaristan who worked in Baghdad. He followed the Shafi'i school for nearly a decade, then developed his own school of law (the Jariri school), which lasted about two centuries after him. He is best known for his Qur'an commentary, Tafsir al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan), and his historical chronicle. What: Al-Tabari's 2:275 treatment opens with the philology of riba — 'increase upon a thing' — and the pre-Islamic practice of doubling a debt for extra term, then draws the line: profit from sale is permitted trade, increase on a debt for time is the forbidden riba. The distinction every murabaha manual rests on. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 923 (year of the author's death). Source: Jami' al-Bayan (Tafsir al-Tabari), on Q2:275.

rows.name: al-Qurtubi
rows.detail: Al-Qurtubi develops the same trade/riba reading of 2:275 with the Maliki legal detail.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Qurtubi (1214-1273) was an Andalusian Maliki jurist and Qur'an commentator, taught by the scholars of Cordoba; after the city fell in 1236 he moved to Egypt. His twenty-volume commentary, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an (Tafsir al-Qurtubi), is a general commentary written from a Maliki point of view. What: Al-Qurtubi's 2:275 commentary works the trade/riba boundary into Maliki rulings on valid sale forms — the ahkam frame later cost-plus manuals cite. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 1273 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an, on Q2:275.

rows.name: Ibn Kathir
rows.detail: Ibn Kathir on 2:275: the trade/riba divide as the frontier between lawful acquisition and 'illegally acquiring people's money'.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Kathir (1301-1373) of Damascus was a Qur'an commentator, historian and scholar, an expert in tafsir, history and fiqh. A Shafi'i, he is known for a commentary that takes a critical approach to Isra'iliyyat (stories taken from earlier communities). What: Ibn Kathir on 2:275 frames riba-eaters as those who 'illegally acquire people's money, using various evil methods and wicked ways', against the permitted path of trade — the moral casing around the verse murabaha relies on. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 1373 (year of the author's death). Source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir, on Q2:275.

rows.name: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani
rows.detail: Ma'ariful Qur'an on 4:29: the protection of property and the consent rule as the gate every sale — murabaha included — must pass.
rows.detail_long: Who: Mufti Muhammad Shafi Usmani (1897-1976) was born in Deoband, became chief mufti of Darul Uloom Deoband in 1931, and later Grand Mufti of Pakistan in Karachi. His best-known work, Ma'ariful Qur'an, is an Urdu commentary on the whole Qur'an that began as a decade of weekly radio lectures. He belonged to the Hanafi school and the Deobandi movement. What: Ma'ariful Qur'an on 4:29 sets the verse in its Surah al-Nisa' sequence: guarding rights and property, then forbidding wrongful consumption of wealth — with trade by mutual consent as the lawful channel. Why here: 'Qur'an commentary (tafsir)' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1976 (year of the author's death). Source: Ma'ariful Qur'an, on Q4:29.

rows.timeline_year_basis: Year of the author's death; the Muwatta is the earliest surviving school literature
rows.name: Imam Malik ibn Anas
rows.detail: Al-Muwatta. The earliest juristic murabaha text in the Gold Ark Library: Malik rules which costs may enter the murabaha base and which may not.
rows.detail_long: Who: Malik ibn Anas (711-795), called the Imam of Medina, is the eponym of the Maliki school, one of the four Sunni schools of law; the school became the norm in much of North Africa and al-Andalus. Al-Muwatta is his work. Al-Shafi'i was his best-known student. What: Muwatta 1425: transporting goods enters the cost base; the trader's own labour, ironing, folding, house rent do not — unless disclosed to and accepted by the buyer. Bleaching, tailoring, dyeing count like the goods. Undisclosed items void the profit claim; if the goods are gone, transport is reimbursed without profit; if not gone, the sale is void unless renegotiated. Murabaha arrives in law fully formed as a DISCLOSURE doctrine. CONTEXT: no Sunni prophetic hadith names murabaha — the contract enters the tradition through juristic literature; this Muwatta chapter is that entry point. Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Maliki voice; shown at 795 (year of the author's death; the Muwatta is the earliest surviving school literature). Source: Al-Muwatta 1425, Business Transactions.

rows.name: al-Shafi'i
rows.detail: Al-Shafi'i's Kitab al-Umm holds the seminal passage: a lawful cost-plus resale — the trust-sale foundation of bank murabaha.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Shafi'i (767-820) was a jurist, a student of Malik, and the eponym of the Shafi'i school. He is known as the first to write a book on the principles of jurisprudence, al-Risala. What: The al-Umm passage ('buy this and I will give you a profit — this deal is lawful') is the text Sami Hamoud later builds three-party bank murabaha on. In the work itself (vol. and page 3:39; our literal translation from the Arabic): “And if the man shows the man the goods and says: buy this and I will give you a profit on it of such; and the man buys it; then the purchase is permissible, and the one who said 'I will give you a profit on it' has the option: if he wishes he makes a new sale in it, and if he wishes he leaves it.” It also states: “And likewise if he said: buy for me goods - and he described them to him - or goods, whichever goods you wish, and I will give you a profit on them; all of this is the same: the first sale is permissible.” It also states: “The first sale is permissible and the two of them have the option in the other [second] sale; and if they renew it, it is permissible.” It also states: “And if the two contracted the sale on the basis that they bound themselves to the first matter, then it is annulled on account of two things: one of them: that they contracted its sale before the seller owned it.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Shafi'i voice; shown at 820 (year of the author's death). Source: Kitab al-Umm.

rows.name: al-Kasani
rows.detail: Al-Kasani gives the standard definition: sale at the first price plus a disclosed excess as profit.
rows.detail_long: Who: Al-Kasani (d. 587 AH / 1191 CE) was a jurist of the Hanafi school and author of Bada'i al-Sana'i, a work that draws heavily on al-Sarakhsi's al-Mabsut. What: Bada'i al-Sana'i defines murabaha precisely — resale at cost plus declared markup — the definition modern standards still quote. In the work itself (vol. and page 5:220; our literal translation from the Arabic): “(And among them [the conditions]) is that the first price be known in the sale of murabaha, tawliya, ishrak and wadi'a; and the basis for these contracts is the general texts on sale, without distinction between one sale and another.” It also states: “And God, mighty is His affair, said: {and seek of the bounty of God} [al-Jumu'a: 10]. [The page then cites al-Baqara: 198 and says: وَالْمُرَابَحَةُ ابْتِغَاءٌ لِلْفَضْلِ مِنْ الْبَيْعِ نَصًّا - "and murabaha is a seeking of bounty from sale, by text".]” It also states: “Because murabaha is a sale at the first price with an addition of profit, and knowledge of the first price is a condition of the validity of the sales, all of them.” It also states: “And likewise the people have inherited [handed down] these sales in all the ages without objection, and that is a consensus on their permissibility.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1191 (standard references). Source: Bada'i al-Sana'i.

rows.name: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi
rows.detail: Ibn Qudama treats murabaha among the named trust-sales for the Hanbalis; Malikis and Hanafis do likewise.
rows.detail_long: Who: Ibn Qudama al-Maqdisi (1147-1223) was a jurist of the Hanbali school who studied in Baghdad and taught in Damascus; he is regarded as one of the school's most authoritative classical figures. He is best known for al-Mughni, a legal encyclopedia that compares the opinions of the Sunni schools while setting out the Hanbali position in detail. He also wrote 'Umdat al-Fiqh. What: Al-Mughni files murabaha with tawliya and wadi'a as buyu' al-amanah (trust sales) — valid when cost is truthfully disclosed. In the work itself (vol. and page 4:136; our literal translation from the Arabic): “The meaning of the murabaha sale: it is the sale at the capital [cost] and a known profit; and the knowledge of both of them of the capital is a condition; so he says: my capital in it, or it stands me at, a hundred; I have sold it to you at it, and a profit of ten. So this is permissible; there is no disagreement about its validity.” It also states: “And if he said: I have sold it to you at my capital in it, and it is a hundred, and I profit a dirham on every ten; or he said: 'dah yazdah', or 'dah davazdah' [Persian: ten-eleven, ten-twelve] - then Ahmad disliked it.” It also states: “And Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Sirin, Shurayh, al-Nakha'i, al-Thawri, al-Shafi'i, the People of Opinion [ashab al-ra'y] and Ibn al-Mundhir allowed a concession in it.” Why here: 'Classical law schools' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Hanbali voice; shown at 1223 (year of the author's death). Source: Al-Mughni.

rows.name: Sami Hassan Hamoud
rows.detail: Sami Hamoud engineers 'Murabaha to the Purchase Orderer' in his Cairo PhD — the bank three-party structure.
rows.detail_long: Who: Sami Hassan Hamoud was a Jordanian scholar and banker linked with Jordan Islamic Bank, credited with the murabaha-to-the-purchase-orderer banking model. His birth and death years differ between sources, so none is shown. What: His thesis Tatwir al-A'mal al-Masrifiyya grounds bank murabaha on al-Shafi'i's al-Umm passage and recommends it to the Islamic Development Bank and Dubai Islamic Bank — the single most consequential piece of modern financial ijtihad. In the source's own words (Penn Libraries catalogue record - Tatwir al-a'mal al-masrifiyah bi-ma yattafiqu wa-al-shari'ah al-Islamiyah / Sami Hasan Ahmad Hammud): “Author/Creator: Ḥammūd, Sāmī Ḥasan Aḥmad, 1938-” “Edition: al-Ṭabʻah 1. Place of Publication: [Cairo] : S.Ḥ.A. Ḥammūd, 1976.” “Originally presented as the auther's Thesis (doctoral)--Jāmiʻat al-Qāhirah, 1976.” “Physical Description: 7, 552 pages ; 24 cm” Not confirmed by the source read: No page read says he 'engineered' or first proposed 'murabaha to the purchase orderer'. The catalogue records do not mention murabaha at all. They do not name a school. IsDB Prize page for him: Not found. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Murabaha ladder, Hanafi voice; shown at 1976 (PhD thesis year). Source: Tatwir al-A'mal al-Masrifiyya.

rows.name: OIC Fiqh Academy
rows.detail: OIC Resolutions 40-41 make the customer's promise binding — the legal key to bank murabaha.
rows.detail_long: Who: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC issues numbered resolutions at its sessions; AAOIFI's standards cite them. What: The 5th-session resolutions settle that a unilateral promise to purchase can be made binding, closing the gap that made three-party murabaha legally fragile. In the source's own words (International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC) - Resolution Nos. 40-41 (2/5 and 3/5) Keeping a Promise and Murabahah to the Purchase Orderer): “First: Murabahah to the purchase orderer is permissible on goods that are already in the physical possession of the seller, as required by Shariah, provided the seller carries the risk of loss before delivery” “a promise (made unilaterally by the purchase orderer or the seller), is morally binding on the promisor, unless there is a valid excuse.” “It is however legally binding if made conditional upon the fulfillment of an obligation, and the promisee has already incurred expenses on the basis of such a promise.” “Third: Mutual promise (involving two parties) is permissible in the case of Murabahah sale provided that the option is given to one or both parties. Without such an option, it is not permissible” Not confirmed by the source read: It does not say the customer's promise is simply 'binding'. It says a unilateral promise is morally binding, and legally binding only if conditional on an obligation and the promisee has incurred expenses. A mutual binding promise without an option is 'not permissible'. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 1988 (5th session, Kuwait, 1988). Source: OIC Resolutions 40-41 make the customer's promise binding.

rows.name: OIC Fiqh Academy
rows.detail: OIC Fiqh Academy declares organized tawarruq (reverse murabaha) impermissible.
rows.detail_long: Who: The International Islamic Fiqh Academy of the OIC issues numbered resolutions at its sessions; AAOIFI's standards cite them. What: Organized tawarruq — murabaha chains engineered purely to generate cash — is ruled a hiyal (legal artifice) defeating the contract's purpose. In the source's own words (International Islamic Fiqh Academy (OIC) - Resolution No. 179 (5/19) Essence and Types of Tawaruq (Fiqh Compliant vs Bank Structured)): “Structured and inverse tawaruq are prohibited because they involve explicit, implicit or customary collusion between financer and finance seeker (mustawriq)” “Inverse tawaruq takes the same form of structured tawaruq except that the mustawriq is the institution, and the financer is the client.” “This form of tawaruq is permitted by Shariah, provided that it satisfies Shariah-acceptable conditions of sale.” “Having reviewed the resolutions of the Islamic Fiqh Council of the Muslim World League, Makkah al-Mukarramah, regarding this subject,” Not confirmed by the source read: The OIC Academy page prints 2009 (Sharjah), not 2003. It does not call organised tawarruq 'reverse murabaha'; 'inverse tawaruq' is printed as a separate type (institution is the mustawriq). The page gives no date for the Muslim World League resolutions it mentions. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 2003 (session date). Source: OIC Fiqh Academy declares organized tawarruq (reverse murabaha) impermissible.

rows.name: AAOIFI
rows.detail: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 8 codifies murabaha for the industry.
rows.detail_long: Who: AAOIFI (the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions) issues the Shari'ah Standards. They are mandatory in Bahrain, its home jurisdiction, and adopted in the UAE and other countries. What: SS8 sets the documentation, sequence-of-ownership and promise rules for murabaha and murabaha-to-the-purchase-orderer. Adoption: rules adopted 31 May 2000, reformatted as Standard 16 May 2002. Clauses read in the standard's text: 3/1/1 — the Institution shall not sell any item in a murabaha transaction before it acquires it (ownership-before-sale); 4/1 — no commitment fee may be taken from the customer; 4/3 — contract-document expenses borne evenly by both parties. Why here: 'Modern rules & standards' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 2002 (adopted as Shari'ah *rules* 29-31 May 2000 (meeting 4); readopted as a Standard at meeting 8, 11-16 May 2002). Source: AAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 8.

rows.name: Industry practice
rows.detail: Murabaha dominates bank financing — 80-90% of some banks' operations, >55% GCC average (2016) — and is the most criticized structure.
rows.detail_long: Who: This rung is a snapshot of how the contract is used in the market today. It is a description of practice, not a ruling. What: Estimates put murabaha at over half of all Islamic financing. Abdullah Saeed and others criticize it as economically replicating interest; defenders answer that ownership risk and asset-backing distinguish it. Not found: No primary source page was found or opened that prints '80-90% of some banks' operations' or '>55% GCC average (2016)'. Why here: 'Today' rung of the Murabaha ladder; shown at 2024 (current practice window). Source: Industry practice / IFSB data.
